npdar

Overview

npdar provides R utilities for the National Paediatric Diabetes Audit (NPDA), developed and maintained by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH).

The package supports:

  • Blood pressure assessment: calculate expected values, z-scores and percentiles, and categorise blood pressure using paediatric or adult references.

  • Statistical utilities:

    1. mask small counts and apply secondary suppression to reduce the risk of back-calculation for data privacy;

    2. identify first/last/most recent modal values or first/last entry in a longitudinal record with options to ignore specific values;

    3. summarise categorical measure(s) by group(s) with counts, denominators and percentages in long format for easy use in ggplot2 and plotly.

  • Audit period identification: identify audit/fiscal years and quarters using a configurable first-quarter start month.

  • Correlation visualisation: create interactive correlation matrix with plotly and stats::cor().

See the package documentation for full function references and examples.

Disclaimer ⚠️

This package is designed for:

  • Assisting NPDA data analysis.
  • Improving transparency and reproducibility of NPDA analysis.
  • Helping other research and epidemiological analysis.

This package is NOT:

  • A clinical decision support or diagnosis tool.
  • Approved for use in clinical care pathways.

Healthcare professionals must use validated clinical tools and their professional judgement when making patient care decisions. The blood pressure categorisation functions implement published research guidelines (NHBPEP Fourth Report, NICE/BHF guidances) for audit analysis purposes only, not for clinical use.

Installation

npdar is not currently available on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub using pak:

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("rcpch/npdar")

# devtools::install_github() was deprecated 
# in favour of pak::pak() since devtools 2.5.0
# install.packages("devtools")
# devtools::install_github("rcpch/npdar")

Alternatively, use remotes:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("rcpch/npdar")

Quick Start 

library(npdar)

Blood Pressure

It’s recommended to use the NHBPEP Fourth Report reference for children and adolescents aged 0-17 years. Height must already be expressed as a z-score, not in centimetres or other units. bp_assess() returns a tibble with the expected BP, z-score, percentile and category. The 25-year-old below is outside this reference’s age range, so returns NA.

bp_assess(
  bp_value = c(95, 125, 155),
  bp_type = "systolic",
  sex = c(1, 2, 1),
  male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
  height_z = c(0, 0.5, -0.5),
  age_years = c(10, 15, 25),
  ref = "Fourth Report"
)
#> Ignore 1 age(s) outside 0-17 years. NHBPEP Fourth Report is only designed for children <= 17 years.
#> NHBPEP Fourth Report categorise 'Normotension' to 'Stage 2 hypertension'; Special rules for newborns (<1), children (0-12), adolescents (12-17).
#> BP outside National Paediatric Diabetes Audit (NPDA) limit removed unless acceptable range is explicitly specified by 'bp_limit'.
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   expected zscore percentile category       
#>      <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>          
#> 1     102. -0.672       25.1 Normotension   
#> 2     112.  1.28        90.0 Prehypertension
#> 3      NA  NA           NA   <NA>

For adults older than 17 years, it’s recommended to select the NICE/BHF reference explicitly. Ages outside the selected reference range return NA, and only category is defined for adults.

bp_assess(
  bp_value = c(155, 155),
  bp_type = "systolic",
  sex = c(1, 1),
  male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
  height_z = c(0, 0),
  age_years = c(15, 25),
  ref = "NICE/BHF"
)
#> Ignore 1 age(s) ≤ 17 years. NPDA only uses NICE/BHF reference for (young) adults >17 years.
#> NICE/BHF only provides category guidelines, expected BP and zscore/percentile BP not calculated.
#> NICE/BHF categorise 'Normotension' to 'Stage 3 hypertension'.
#> BP outside National Diabetes Audit (NDA) limit removed unless acceptable range is explicitly specified by 'bp_limit'.
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   expected zscore percentile category            
#>      <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>               
#> 1       NA     NA         NA <NA>                
#> 2       NA     NA         NA Stage 1 hypertension

Apart from the bp_assess() function, bp_category(), bp_relative(), and bp_expected() can be used separately to compute only the category, z score, percentile, or expected value respectively.

bp_category(
  bp_value = c(155, 155),
  bp_type = "systolic",
  sex = c(1, 1),
  male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
  height_z = c(0, 0),
  age_years = c(15, 25),
  ref = "NICE/BHF",
  .quiet = TRUE
)
#> [1] NA                     "Stage 1 hypertension"

The bp_family functions can be used in a dplyr pipeline nicely.

df <- data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  sex = c(1, 2, 1),
  height_z = c(0, 0.5, -0.5),
  age_years = c(10, 15, 25),
  sbp = c(95, 125, 155)
)

df |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sbp_z = bp_relative(
      bp_value = sbp, bp_type = "systolic",
      sex = sex, 
      male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
      height_z = height_z, 
      age_years = age_years,
      ref = "Fourth",
      .quiet = FALSE)$zscore
  )
#> Ignore 1 age(s) outside 0-17 years. NHBPEP Fourth Report is only designed for children <= 17 years.
#>   id sex height_z age_years sbp      sbp_z
#> 1  1   1      0.0        10  95 -0.6718766
#> 2  2   2      0.5        15 125  1.2830761
#> 3  3   1     -0.5        25 155         NA

Privacy Masking

By default, get_masked() masks positive counts below 3 and leaves zeros unchanged. If only one count is masked, all occurrences of the next smallest positive value are also masked to prevent back-calculation. The result is a character vector. Here only 2 is below 3, so the 4s are masked as well.

get_masked(c(4, 6, 2, 4, 0, 5, 5))
#> [1] "masked" "6"      "masked" "masked" "0"      "5"      "5"

Customise the threshold and the suppression label:

get_masked(c(4, 6, 2, 4, 0, 5, 5), threshold = 5, mask_label = "*")
#> [1] "*" "6" "*" "*" "0" "5" "5"
get_masked(c(4, 6, 2, 4, 0, 5, 5), threshold = 6, mask_label = "*")
#> [1] "*" "6" "*" "*" "0" "*" "*"

Longitudinal Summaries

get_ultimate() uses vector order, so sort longitudinal records chronologically before selecting a most recent value. These examples exclude unknown and missing values and deliberately include tied modes; warnings explain which modes were not selected.

dat_long <- c("A", "B", "C", "A", "A", "Unknown", "Unknown",
          NA, "C", "C", "B", "B", "Unknown")

Select the tied mode that occurs most recently:

get_ultimate(dat_long, find = "uptodate_mode", exclude = c("Unknown", NA))
#> Warning in get_ultimate(dat_long, find = "uptodate_mode", exclude =
#> c("Unknown", : There are multiple modes, the remaining modes are: A, C
#> [1] "B"

Use the package’s last_mode rule instead:

get_ultimate(dat_long, find = "last_mode", exclude = c("Unknown", NA))
#> Warning in get_ultimate(dat_long, find = "last_mode", exclude = c("Unknown", :
#> There are multiple modes, the remaining modes are: A, B
#> [1] "C"

Categorical Frequencies

The following examples use synthetic data. get_frequency() returns a long table with a numerator, denominator and proportion (percent, on a 0-1 scale) for each category. Missing measure values are excluded by default; use count_na = TRUE to include them.

set.seed(1999)
dat_survey1 <- data.frame(
  participant_id = seq_len(60),
  country = rep(c("England", "Wales"), each = 30),
  region = rep(
    c("East England", "West England", NA, "North Wales", "South Wales", NA),
    each = 10
  ),
  q1_catq = sample(c("A", "B", "C", NA), 60, replace = TRUE),
  q2_catq = sample(c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", NA), 60, replace = TRUE)
)

dat_survey2 <- data.frame(
  auditYear = c(rep(2021, 3), rep(2022, 3), rep(2023, 6)),
  sex = c(
    "Female", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Male",
    "Female", "Male", "Male", "Male", NA, NA
  ),
  type = c("A", "B", "B", "A", "B", NA,
           sample(c("A", "B", NA), 6, replace = TRUE))
)

Separate Group Summary

With nested = FALSE (the default), each grouping variable is summarised separately. The special group name "overall" adds an overall summary.

sum_freq_eg1 <- get_frequency(
  data = dat_survey1,
  measures = c("q1_catq", "q2_catq"),
  groups = c("overall", "country", "region")
)

sum_freq_eg1 |>
  dplyr::filter(category == "A")
#> # A tibble: 14 × 8
#>    overall country region       measure category numerator denominator percent
#>    <chr>   <chr>   <chr>        <chr>   <chr>        <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1 overall <NA>    <NA>         q1_catq A               10          41  0.244 
#>  2 overall <NA>    <NA>         q2_catq A                9          54  0.167 
#>  3 <NA>    England <NA>         q1_catq A                5          21  0.238 
#>  4 <NA>    England <NA>         q2_catq A                1          28  0.0357
#>  5 <NA>    Wales   <NA>         q1_catq A                5          20  0.25  
#>  6 <NA>    Wales   <NA>         q2_catq A                8          26  0.308 
#>  7 <NA>    <NA>    East England q1_catq A                2           7  0.286 
#>  8 <NA>    <NA>    East England q2_catq A                0           9  0     
#>  9 <NA>    <NA>    North Wales  q1_catq A                1           7  0.143 
#> 10 <NA>    <NA>    North Wales  q2_catq A                4          10  0.4   
#> 11 <NA>    <NA>    South Wales  q1_catq A                3           9  0.333 
#> 12 <NA>    <NA>    South Wales  q2_catq A                2           9  0.222 
#> 13 <NA>    <NA>    West England q1_catq A                1           7  0.143 
#> 14 <NA>    <NA>    West England q2_catq A                1          10  0.1

Nested Group Summary

Use nested = TRUE to summarise combinations of grouping variables, such as sex within each audit year:

get_frequency(
  data = dat_survey2,
  measures = "type",
  groups = c("auditYear", "sex"),
  nested = TRUE
)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 7
#>    auditYear sex    measure category numerator denominator percent
#>        <dbl> <chr>  <chr>   <chr>        <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1      2021 Female type    A                1           2     0.5
#>  2      2021 Female type    B                1           2     0.5
#>  3      2021 Male   type    A                0           1     0  
#>  4      2021 Male   type    B                1           1     1  
#>  5      2022 Female type    A                1           1     1  
#>  6      2022 Female type    B                0           1     0  
#>  7      2022 Male   type    A                0           1     0  
#>  8      2022 Male   type    B                1           1     1  
#>  9      2023 Female type    A                0           1     0  
#> 10      2023 Female type    B                1           1     1  
#> 11      2023 Male   type    A                0           2     0  
#> 12      2023 Male   type    B                2           2     1

Count NAs

Use count_na = TRUE to include missing values in the denominator and report them as a separate NA category (only for measures that contain missing values).

sum_freq_eg3 <- get_frequency(
  data = dat_survey1,
  measures = "q1_catq",
  groups = c("country", "region"),
  nested = TRUE,
  count_na = TRUE
)

sum_freq_eg3 |>
  dplyr::filter(region %in% c("East England", "North Wales"))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 7
#>   country region       measure category numerator denominator percent
#>   <chr>   <chr>        <chr>   <chr>        <int>       <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 England East England q1_catq A                2          10     0.2
#> 2 England East England q1_catq B                4          10     0.4
#> 3 England East England q1_catq C                1          10     0.1
#> 4 England East England q1_catq <NA>             3          10     0.3
#> 5 Wales   North Wales  q1_catq A                1          10     0.1
#> 6 Wales   North Wales  q1_catq B                2          10     0.2
#> 7 Wales   North Wales  q1_catq C                4          10     0.4
#> 8 Wales   North Wales  q1_catq <NA>             3          10     0.3

Static Plot with ggplot2 

library(ggplot2)

sum_freq_eg1 |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(country)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = percent, fill = category)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Country", y = "Percent", fill = "Category")

Interactive Plot with plotly 

library(plotly)

sum_freq_eg1 |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(country)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(measure) |>
  dplyr::group_map(\(df, ...) {
    plot_ly(df, x = ~country, y = ~percent, 
            color = ~category, type = "bar")
  }) |>
  subplot(nrows = 1, shareX = TRUE, shareY = TRUE)

Audit Periods

The default audit year starts in April. With no date supplied, audit_year() uses today’s date:

audit_year()
#> [1] "2026/27 Q3"

Fixed dates keep the rendered examples reproducible:

audit_year("2025-03-31")
#> [1] "2024/25 Q4"
audit_year("2025-03-31", format = FALSE)
#> [1] 2024

Change the first-quarter start month for a different audit calendar:

audit_year("2025-03-31", start_month = 1)
#> [1] "2025/26 Q1"

Generate an inclusive sequence of audit years:

data.frame(
  audit_year = audit_year_range(2010, 2015),
  audit_year_numeric = audit_year_range(2010, 2015, format = FALSE)
)
#>   audit_year audit_year_numeric
#> 1    2010/11               2010
#> 2    2011/12               2011
#> 3    2012/13               2012
#> 4    2013/14               2013
#> 5    2014/15               2014
#> 6    2015/16               2015

Correlation Matrix with plotly

plot_corr_matrix() creates an interactive lower-triangle correlation heatmap. Supply a data frame containing only numeric variables:

plot_corr_matrix(mtcars)

Customise the plot, for example by selecting Spearman correlations, hiding the values and customising the colour bar:

plot_corr_matrix(
  mtcars,
  method = "spearman",
  show_values = FALSE,
  show_stars = TRUE,
  colorbar = list(title = "Spearman Corr")
) |>
  plotly::layout(
    margin = list(b = 80),
    annotations = list(list(
      text = paste0("<i><b>Note:</b> *: p<0.05, **: p<0.01, ***: p<0.001.</i>"),
      x = 1, y = -0.15, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
      xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top",
      showarrow = FALSE
    ))
  )
